prompt: Which of the following claims is most consistent with Scientist 1's viewpoint?

choices.text: A fixed magnetic reference is needed because the sun moves.
choices.rationale: This is Scientist 2's argument.

choices.text: Magnetite grains in the abdomen guide bees back to the hive.
choices.rationale: Magnetite is part of Scientist 2's explanation.

choices.text: Bees navigate just as well in complete darkness as in daylight.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 says bees kept in the dark become misdirected, and overcast days cause failures.

choices.text: Bees can detect the direction of polarized light in the sky.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 1 says bees read the pattern of polarized light even when the sun is hidden.

explanation: Polarized-light detection is central to Scientist 1's sun-compass view.

stimulus.title: How Bees Find Their Way
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Honeybees find their way home using the sun. A forager keeps track of the angle between its flight path and the sun, and it can read the pattern of polarized light in the sky even when the sun itself is hidden by clouds. Bees kept in the dark for several hours and then released set off in a direction shifted by the amount the sun has moved, showing that they steer by a remembered sun position. On fully overcast days with no polarized light, foragers often fail to return. Bees are also known to communicate the direction of food relative to the sun, which would be pointless unless the sun were their compass.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Bees rely mainly on Earth's magnetic field. Bees contain tiny grains of magnetite, an iron mineral that responds to magnetic fields, in their abdomens. In experiments, bees trained to find sugar water in one direction lost the ability when a small magnet was attached to them, and hives placed between strong electrical coils that disturbed the field produced disorganized combs. The sun is useful, but it moves across the sky and disappears at night and on cloudy days, so a fixed magnetic reference is needed. Bees that return home on overcast days are using the field, not the sky.

prompt: Both scientists would most likely agree that:

choices.text: the beetles are the underlying cause of the trees' death.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 calls drought the underlying cause.

choices.text: rainfall on the ridge has been below average for most of the past eight years.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 omits this; Scientist 2 asserts it, and Scientist 1 does not mention rainfall.

choices.text: bark beetles are attacking the pines on the ridge.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both describe beetle attacks; Scientist 2 calls them the final blow.

choices.text: removing infested trees would protect the rest of the stand.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says removal will not save the others.

explanation: The beetle attacks are common ground; whether they are cause or consequence is disputed.

stimulus.title: The Dying Pines
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The pines on the ridge are dying because of bark beetles. The beetles bore through the bark and lay eggs, and their larvae eat the living layer beneath, cutting off the flow of water and sugar. Every dead tree examined shows the winding galleries the larvae leave, and traps caught ten times more beetles this year than five years ago. Warm winters now let the beetles survive and produce two generations in a summer instead of one. Healthy trees can drown attacking beetles in resin, but a mass attack overwhelms even vigorous trees. Removing infested trees before the beetles emerge is the way to protect the rest of the stand.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The underlying cause is drought. Rainfall on the ridge has been below average for six of the past eight years, and the soil there is thin and holds little water. A tree short of water cannot make enough resin to repel beetles, so the insects succeed on trees that would normally resist them. Trees on the well-watered lower slopes carry the same beetles yet remain mostly alive, and tree rings from the dead pines show narrow growth for several years before the beetles arrived. Beetles are the final blow, not the cause. Unless the drought ends or the stand is thinned so that fewer trees compete for water, removing infested trees will not save the others.

prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 1's viewpoint?

choices.text: The crust is found to be thicker, and able to hold far more water, than earlier estimates had suggested.
choices.rationale: A larger crustal reservoir supports Scientist 2.

choices.text: Clay minerals cover a larger fraction of the surface than previously mapped.
choices.rationale: More clay supports Scientist 2.

choices.text: Rover drilling finds water bound in rock at every site sampled.
choices.rationale: Widespread bound water supports Scientist 2.

choices.text: The rate of hydrogen escape from Mars was hundreds of times higher in the past than it is today.
choices.rationale: Correct. Much faster escape in the past answers Scientist 2's objection that escape is too slow.

explanation: Scientist 2's main objection is that escape is too slow; evidence of much faster past escape removes it.

stimulus.title: Where Mars's Water Went
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Mars once had rivers and lakes, and most of that water escaped to space. Early in its history Mars lost its global magnetic field, which had shielded the atmosphere from the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. Without that shield, the particles stripped gas from the top of the atmosphere, and the planet's weak gravity could not hold it back. As the air thinned, surface water boiled or froze, and water vapor rising into the upper atmosphere was broken apart by sunlight, with the light hydrogen escaping. A spacecraft orbiting Mars today still measures hydrogen and oxygen leaking away, and the ratio of heavy to light hydrogen in the remaining water shows that most of the original water is gone.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Most of the water never left; it is locked inside the crust. When water reacts with volcanic rock, it becomes part of the minerals that form, such as clays. Orbiting instruments have found such water-bearing minerals across large areas of the Martian surface, and rovers have measured water bound in the rocks they drill. Calculations of how much water those minerals can hold suggest that the crust could contain an ocean's worth. Escape to space is real but slow, and at the rates measured today it cannot account for the amount of water the early rivers required. Mars dried out mainly because its water was absorbed by the ground.

prompt: Suppose a lake with heavy fertilizer runoff and summer algae blooms but no zander were found to have a stable perch population. This finding would most likely:

choices.text: weaken Scientist 1's explanation.
choices.rationale: Correct. If blooms and runoff occur without a decline, they are unlikely to be sufficient to cause one.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2's explanation.
choices.rationale: A lake with no zander and no decline is consistent with Scientist 2's view.

choices.text: support Scientist 1's explanation.
choices.rationale: The finding shows runoff and blooms without a decline, the opposite of what Scientist 1 predicts.

choices.text: support both explanations equally.
choices.rationale: The finding favors the predation explanation over the oxygen explanation.

explanation: Scientist 1 predicts that runoff and blooms cause decline; a counterexample weakens that prediction.

stimulus.title: The Perch of Miller Lake
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The decline of perch in Miller Lake began soon after the farms upstream expanded. Fertilizer washed into the lake by rain feeds algae, which bloom across the surface each summer. When the algae die, bacteria decompose them and use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Measurements taken in August show oxygen levels near the bottom of the lake that are too low for perch eggs and young fish to survive. Adult perch can move to shallower water, but their young cannot, so each year fewer fish reach adulthood. Reducing fertilizer runoff would allow the oxygen to recover and the perch population to rebuild.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The perch decline is due to the arrival of the zander, a predatory fish first recorded in Miller Lake eight years ago, probably released by anglers. Zander feed heavily on young perch, and their numbers have grown each year while the perch count has fallen. Low oxygen alone cannot explain the pattern: the lake had algae blooms for decades before perch began to decline, and nearby lakes with similar farms and blooms still have healthy perch populations but no zander. Stomach samples from zander in the lake contain mostly young perch. Removing zander by netting would allow the perch to recover even if the fertilizer runoff continued.

prompt: The two viewpoints differ mainly about:

choices.text: whether temperature or water quality was the decisive cause.
choices.rationale: Correct. Warm water versus runoff is the central dispute.

choices.text: whether the reef actually bleached during the summer in question.
choices.rationale: Both accept that the bleaching occurred.

choices.text: whether corals depend on algae that live inside their tissues.
choices.rationale: Neither scientist disputes the coral-algae partnership.

choices.text: whether heavy rains fell on the coast in the months before the bleaching.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not dispute the rains, only their importance.

explanation: The disagreement is about the decisive cause, not about the event or the biology.

stimulus.title: The Bleaching Reef
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The reef bleached because the water became too warm. Corals live with tiny algae inside their tissues that supply most of their food and give them their color. When water temperature stays more than about one degree above the summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down: the coral expels the algae and turns white. Satellite records show that the sea surface over the reef was unusually warm for six weeks before the bleaching, and the most heavily bleached patches were in shallow water, where the water warmed most. Reefs far from any town or farm bleached in the same weeks, which only a regional cause such as temperature can explain.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The main cause was runoff from the land. Heavy rains in the months before the bleaching carried soil, fertilizer, and sewage from the coast onto the reef. Sediment clouds the water and settles on the corals, smothering them, while nutrients feed seaweeds that overgrow the coral and bacteria that attack its tissue. Water samples near the river mouth showed nutrient levels several times higher than normal, and bleaching was most severe on the parts of the reef closest to the river. Warm water can stress corals, but these corals had survived warmer summers before. The difference this year was the condition of the water, not its temperature alone.

prompt: Which of the following is an assumption made by both scientists? Both assume that:

choices.text: the bleaching was caused by the reef's environment rather than by a disease of the corals.
choices.rationale: Correct. Each explanation names an environmental change; neither considers an internal disease of the coral.

choices.text: sediment from the river reached every part of the reef.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 2 discusses sediment, and only near the river.

choices.text: the water over the reef was warmer during the bleaching year than in any previous summer on record.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 says the corals had survived warmer summers.

choices.text: the corals will not recover once they have bleached.
choices.rationale: Neither scientist discusses recovery.

explanation: Both explanations look outside the coral for the cause, taking for granted that an environmental change is responsible.

prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken Scientist 1's viewpoint?

choices.text: Trails on the playa point in the direction of the prevailing wind.
choices.rationale: Trail direction is Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: The playa surface becomes slick after rain.
choices.rationale: Slick mud is part of Scientist 1's account.

choices.text: Rocks are found sitting in grooves pressed into the mud exactly as wide as the rocks themselves.
choices.rationale: The grooves are Scientist 1's own evidence.

choices.text: In wind-tunnel tests, 150 km/h winds fail to budge a 5 kg rock resting on wet playa clay.
choices.rationale: Correct. If even very strong wind cannot move a rock on wet clay, wind alone cannot be the cause.

explanation: Scientist 1's mechanism is wind force on slick mud; a direct test showing wind cannot move the rocks contradicts it.

stimulus.title: The Sliding Stones
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The rocks on the dry lake bed move because of wind on wet mud. After a rare rain, a thin film of water turns the surface of the playa into slick clay. Strong winds, which often exceed 100 km per hour across the flat basin, push the rocks across this slippery surface, and the rocks leave the long trails that puzzle visitors. The trails all point in the direction of the strongest winds, and rocks of similar size on the same part of the playa travel the same distance, which is what wind alone would produce. Rocks are found sitting in shallow mud grooves exactly as wide as themselves, showing they were pressed down into soft mud as they slid.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
Wind on wet mud cannot move rocks that weigh several kilograms; the drag is far too small. The rocks move when thin sheets of ice form on shallow water that floods the playa on cold winter nights. As the ice breaks up in the morning sun, light winds push large floating panels of ice, and the rocks frozen into them or shoved by them slide along. Ice explains why some trails are parallel to one another, as if the rocks moved together, and why the rocks move only in winter. Trails that turn sharply at the same point were made by rocks carried by a single rotating panel of ice.

Scientist 3
The trails are made by flash floods. When heavy rain falls on the surrounding mountains, a sheet of fast water sweeps across the playa, carrying mud and small stones and dragging larger rocks along the bottom. The water drains within hours, leaving the trails in the mud. Floods explain why the trails start and stop abruptly and why loose gravel is sometimes found piled on the downstream side of a rock. Both wind and ice would act on every rock on the playa, yet only some rocks move each year, and those rocks are the ones that lie in the shallow channels where floodwater flows fastest.

prompt: Scientist 2 would most likely agree with which of the following statements?

choices.text: Plankton near the sunlit surface are easily seen and eaten by fish during the day.
choices.rationale: Visibility to predators is Scientist 1's mechanism.

choices.text: Plankton rise earlier in the evening when fish are removed from a tank.
choices.rationale: The tank experiment is Scientist 1's evidence.

choices.text: A plankton animal uses energy more slowly in cold water than in warm water.
choices.rationale: Correct. Scientist 2's whole argument rests on slower energy use in cold, deep water.

choices.text: The daily migration is weak or absent in lakes that contain no fish.
choices.rationale: Fishless lakes are Scientist 1's evidence.

explanation: Slower metabolism in cold water is the foundation of the energy-saving explanation.

stimulus.title: The Nightly Rise of Plankton
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Tiny animals called zooplankton spend the day hundreds of meters below the surface and rise to feed near the top only after dark because they are hiding from predators. The fish that eat them hunt by sight, so a plankton animal near the sunlit surface in daytime is easily seen and eaten. In the dark depths it is nearly invisible. Experiments in large tanks show that plankton stay deeper when fish are present and rise earlier when fish are removed, even if the light is unchanged. In lakes with no fish, the daily migration is weak or absent. The pattern is a trade-off: the surface offers food, but only the night makes it safe.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The migration is a way of saving energy. Water near the surface is warm, and a cold-blooded animal's body uses up energy faster in warm water. By feeding briefly at the surface and then sinking into cold, deep water, a plankton animal digests its food while burning fuel slowly, so it grows faster on the same amount of food. Measurements show that plankton which migrate convert food into body mass more efficiently than those that remain at the surface. Predators may matter in some lakes, but the migration also occurs in the open ocean where visual predators are scarce, and it follows the daily cycle of light because light sets the animals' internal clock, not because light reveals them.

prompt: Scientist 1 and Scientist 2 would both most likely agree that:

choices.text: the Moon's orbit is not tilted relative to Earth's equator.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 states the orbit is tilted; Scientist 1 does not dispute this.

choices.text: the Moon formed from debris produced by a collision.
choices.rationale: Only Scientist 1 proposes a collision.

choices.text: the Moon's rocks have oxygen isotope ratios similar to Earth's.
choices.rationale: Correct. Both accept the isotope match and offer different explanations for it.

choices.text: the Moon has an iron core as large, relative to its size, as Earth's.
choices.rationale: Both describe the Moon's core as small.

explanation: The isotope similarity is a shared fact; each scientist explains it differently.

stimulus.title: The Origin of the Moon
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The Moon formed when a body about the size of Mars collided with the young Earth. The collision blasted molten rock from Earth's outer layers into orbit, where it quickly gathered into the Moon. This explains why the Moon's rocks match Earth's in the ratios of oxygen isotopes, which differ from one body to another in the solar system. It also explains why the Moon has a very small iron core: the impact stripped mostly rocky material from the outside of the Earth, leaving Earth's iron core behind. The Moon's rocks are also unusually dry, as expected if they were once heated enough to drive off their water.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system and was captured by Earth's gravity as it passed nearby. Capture explains why the Moon is so large compared with Earth; the impact scenario should have left a much smaller moon or none at all, as computer models of similar collisions often show. The matching oxygen isotopes could result from the Moon forming in the same region of the solar system as Earth, from the same raw material. A capture would have left the Moon in a tilted orbit, and the Moon's orbit is indeed tilted relative to Earth's equator. The small core could simply reflect the Moon's original composition.

prompt: Which of the following findings, if true, would most strongly support Scientist 2's viewpoint?

choices.text: Bleaching on the reef began at exactly the moment the water temperature passed the summer maximum.
choices.rationale: Timing tied to temperature supports Scientist 1.

choices.text: Satellite images show the warm water covered the entire region.
choices.rationale: A region-wide warm spell is Scientist 1's evidence.

choices.text: Corals in the shallowest water were the first to turn white.
choices.rationale: Shallow water warms most, which fits Scientist 1's view.

choices.text: Corals on a nearby reef that received no river runoff but the same warm water remained healthy.
choices.rationale: Correct. Same warmth without runoff and no bleaching points to runoff as the decisive factor.

explanation: Scientist 2 needs to show that runoff, not warmth, made the difference; a warm but runoff-free healthy reef does that.

prompt: Suppose that, after milkweed was replanted widely across farmland, the number of monarch eggs and caterpillars rose sharply but the number of adults arriving at the winter forests the following year did not. This finding would most likely:

choices.text: weaken Scientist 1's viewpoint and support Scientist 2's.
choices.rationale: Correct. More milkweed produced more caterpillars but no recovery, so milkweed was not the limiting factor; losses elsewhere, such as in winter, are implicated.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 2's viewpoint and support Scientist 1's.
choices.rationale: The finding shows milkweed restoration did not rebuild the population, the opposite of Scientist 1's prediction.

choices.text: weaken Scientist 3's viewpoint only.
choices.rationale: The finding says nothing specific about insecticides.

choices.text: support all three viewpoints about equally.
choices.rationale: The finding contradicts Scientist 1's prediction.

explanation: If caterpillars become abundant without adults recovering, the bottleneck lies after the caterpillar stage, which fits Scientist 2 better than Scientist 1.

stimulus.title: The Missing Monarchs
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
Monarch butterflies have declined because the plants their caterpillars eat are disappearing. Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed, which once grew between rows of corn and soybeans across the continent. Since farms began planting crops that tolerate weed killers, milkweed has been sprayed out of millions of hectares of farmland. Surveys show milkweed on farmland has fallen by more than half, and the decline in monarchs tracks the loss closely. Fewer plants mean fewer eggs laid and fewer caterpillars surviving to migrate. Restoring milkweed along roadsides and field edges is the most direct way to rebuild the population.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The decline is driven by what happens in winter. Nearly the entire population spends the cold months clustered in a few mountain forests, where dense fir trees shelter them from frost and rain. Illegal logging has thinned those forests, and butterflies in thinned stands freeze during winter storms at several times the rate of those in intact forest. Counts of the winter colonies show the sharpest drops in years with storms following logging. Even with plenty of milkweed, a population that loses most of its adults each winter cannot recover. Protecting the winter forests must come first.

Scientist 3
Neither milkweed loss nor logging explains the full pattern. Monarch numbers fell fastest in regions where milkweed was still common, and some years with mild winters still produced small spring populations. The missing factor is insecticide. Seeds coated with long-lasting insecticides are now planted on most cornfields, and the chemicals spread into nearby milkweed. Caterpillars that eat treated milkweed grow slowly and die at higher rates, and adults exposed to the chemicals lay fewer eggs. The decline began within a few years of the coated seeds coming into wide use, which neither of the other explanations accounts for.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the main point on which the scientists disagree? They disagree about:

choices.text: whether a water main runs beneath the road at the site of the collapse.
choices.rationale: Scientist 1 does not deny the main exists; the dispute is about its role.

choices.text: whether a hole actually opened beneath the surface of Carver Road.
choices.rationale: Both accept that the collapse occurred.

choices.text: whether limestone can be dissolved by slightly acidic water over long periods.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 does not dispute the chemistry, only its relevance here.

choices.text: whether the void beneath the road formed slowly in rock or quickly in soil.
choices.rationale: Correct. Slow dissolving of limestone versus rapid washing of soil is the central dispute.

explanation: The disagreement concerns the process and timescale that created the void.

stimulus.title: The Collapse at Carver Road
stimulus.text:
Scientist 1
The sudden hole that opened beneath Carver Road formed because rainwater slowly dissolved the limestone beneath the surface. Limestone is made of a mineral that dissolves in slightly acidic water, and rain becomes acidic as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil. Over thousands of years, water seeping down through cracks widened them into a cavern. The roof of the cavern thinned until it could no longer hold up the road. Caves and springs are common in the surrounding countryside, and the hole has sheer walls of solid limestone, exactly as expected when a cavern roof gives way.
stimulus.text_b:
Scientist 2
The hole formed because a leaking water main washed away the soil beneath the road. The main, installed sixty years ago, runs directly under the collapse and was found to be cracked. Escaping water carried fine soil particles into a nearby storm drain, leaving a growing void just below the pavement. Limestone caverns take thousands of years to form, but the road showed no sign of sinking until two months before the collapse, soon after water pressure in the main was raised. The hole's walls are mostly loose soil, and the solid rock lies several meters deeper. Repairing the main is the key to preventing another collapse.

prompt: Which of the following is an assumption shared by all three scientists?

choices.text: Logging of the winter forests has had no effect on the butterflies.
choices.rationale: Scientist 2 argues the opposite; the others do not deny an effect.

choices.text: Milkweed on farmland is free of insecticide residue.
choices.rationale: Scientist 3 argues the opposite.

choices.text: The decline has a cause that people could act on to help the population recover.
choices.rationale: Correct. Each scientist proposes a human-caused factor and a remedy, taking for granted that the decline is reversible.

choices.text: The monarch population was larger in the past mainly because winters were colder then.
choices.rationale: No scientist claims colder winters helped the population.

explanation: All three name a human activity as the cause and imply that changing it would help, which assumes the decline can be reversed.

choices.text: Plankton that remain at the surface all day are eaten at a much higher rate than those that migrate downward.
choices.rationale: Higher predation at the surface supports Scientist 1.

choices.text: Fish that eat plankton hunt by sight and feed mostly during daylight.
choices.rationale: Visual daytime predators fit Scientist 1's view.

choices.text: The daily migration is strongest in clear lakes where sunlight penetrates deeply.

choices.text: Plankton in a tank migrate on the same schedule with or without fish, as long as the deep water is colder.
